about: Which writes to a system variable a script engine refuses — the question
§scxml-5.10 and §scxml-B-2-8 answer and that every SCE script engine answers
for itself.
§scxml-5.10: "The Processor MUST cause any attempt to change the value of a
system variable to fail and MUST place the error 'error.execution' on the
internal event queue when such an attempt is made." §scxml-B-2-8 says what
a system variable is in the ECMAScript data model: "an ECMAScript read-only
variable", `_event` "an object with properties for each of the fields" of
§scxml-5.10.1, and `_ioprocessors` "an object with a named property for each
Event I/O processor", each holding a `location`.
The rule these cases hold every engine to, and why that rule:
- REFUSED: rebinding a system variable (`_event`, `_sessionid`, `_name`,
`_ioprocessors`); writing, adding or replacing a property §scxml-B-2-8
defines on one (`_event`'s fields, an `_ioprocessors` entry and its
`location`); and the same writes made through another name for the same
object, which change the same value.
- NOT REFUSED: a write INSIDE the value `_event.data` holds. §scxml-B-2-8
gives `data` no structure ("data can be of any type"), and an ECMAScript
read-only property is a binding that cannot be replaced, not an object
that cannot change: the C++ QuickJS binding, which held this rule before
any other engine (`sce/src/scripting/JSEngine.cpp`, accessors with a
throwing setter per field), leaves the payload writable too. The case is
in the table so that the line is drawn in one place rather than by
whatever each engine happens to do.
A refused write is a script that FAILS, which is what each engine reports
and what the Processor turns into `error.execution` on the internal queue.
Why a table. On 2026-11-07 the Lua engines answered `_event.name = 'x'` by
changing `_event.name`, while QuickJS refused it: the Lua engines bind
`_event` as a plain table and the system variables as plain globals. W3C
tests 322, 326 and 346 ask only for `<assign>` to a whole system variable,
which the Processor refuses before any engine is asked, so no test could see
a member write go through. Each engine is held to this one table rather than
to its own copy.
Each case names the write (`write`, ECMAScript; `write_lua`, its Lua
spelling), whether it is refused, and a condition that must hold afterwards
(`after`, `after_lua`) — the value the write would have changed, read back,
so an engine cannot pass by reporting a failure while the write landed.
Every case runs with the session's system variables (`session`) bound and
`event` as the current event; `event.data` is the payload text handed to the
binding. A control case that must NOT be refused stands beside the refused
ones, so an engine cannot pass by refusing every write.
